claims.text: The initial W–Cu composite contains dispersed W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix.
Standard processing of the initial W–Cu composite produces phase separation.
Standard processing of the initial W–Cu composite produces interfacial voids.
High-pressure spark plasma sintering is used as a single-step modification during fabrication of the W–Cu joint.
High-pressure SPS will produce a graded interface in the W–Cu joint.
High-pressure SPS will increase densification at the W–Cu interface.
The rapid heating used in SPS reduces the time available for diffusion-driven phase separation.
High pressure and rapid heating during SPS suppress interfacial void nucleation.
Reduced phase separation and void formation maintain a continuous thermally conductive path across the interface.
Maintaining a continuous conductive path across the interface enhances the joint's thermal conductivity.
High-pressure-SPS joints will have higher thermal conductivity than conventionally sintered W–Cu joints.
High-pressure-SPS joints will retain more stable thermal conductivity under simulated operational temperatures and irradiation than conventionally sintered joints.
High-pressure-SPS joints will show less phase segregation and interfacial void formation than conventionally sintered joints.
Conventionally sintered W–Cu composites typically have interfacial voids and phase separation.
Interfacial voids and phase separation in conventionally sintered W–Cu composites reduce thermal conductivity.
The intervention is expected to remain beneficial only at SPS temperatures and pressures that do not degrade the constituent materials.
The predicted service benefit is limited to thermal and irradiation exposures below the stability thresholds of the modified interface.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity improvement and the long-term irradiation resistance are uncertain.
